What you need to train alone

  • A ball in your match size (size 5 for teenagers and adults).
  • A wall or rebounder for passing and first touch. A garage door, school wall or fence with a solid panel works if you have permission.
  • 4–6 cones or any markers (shoes, bottles) for turns, dribbling gates and sprint distances.
  • A phone to time sprints, film a set of reps, and keep your log.
  • Space: about 20 m of flat ground for sprints. A park or an empty pitch is ideal.

ops.anchor: How do you progress a soccer training plan over 12 weeks?
ops.html:
Should a soccer training plan include strength and injury prevention?

Yes. A short strength and movement routine two or three times a week is one of the best things you can add, because it helps protect your knees, ankles and hamstrings. It doesn't need a gym: 15 minutes of bodyweight exercises after your warm-up, or as part of it, is enough to start.

There is research behind this. A 2008 trial in Norway (Soligard and colleagues, published in the BMJ) followed 1,892 female players aged 13 to 17 for one league season. Teams that used a structured warm-up for strength, balance and control had fewer injuries overall, fewer overuse injuries and fewer severe injuries than teams that didn't. The drop in leg injuries alone was not statistically clear, so the result is promising but not proof for every player. FIFA's free 11+ warm-up is a well-known routine of this kind you can look up and follow.

ExerciseSets x repsWhat it helps
Bodyweight squats2 x 10–15Leg strength, landing
Forward lunges2 x 8 each legSingle-leg strength and balance
Single-leg balance (eyes open, then closed)2 x 30 s each legAnkle and knee control
Plank and side plank2 x 30 s eachCore strength for shielding and duels
Glute bridge, single leg2 x 10 each legHamstrings and hips

Put it on Monday and Wednesday in the weekly template, never as a hard session the day before a match. If you want to lift weights, learn the movements from a qualified coach first, and stop any exercise that causes pain.

ops.anchor: How do you track progress in your training plan?
ops.html:
How should your plan change in the off-season, pre-season and in-season?

Your plan should follow your season. In-season, matches come first and solo work stays short. Pre-season, you build fitness back up gradually. In the off-season, rest first, then use the free time for your biggest weakness. The weekly template stays the same, only the amount and focus change.

PhaseMain goalSolo sessions a weekFocus
In-seasonPlay well every weekend2–3 shortTouches, game IQ, match review, recovery. Hard work mid-week only.
Off-season (first part)Rest and recover0–2 easyOther sports, pickup games, light touches. The AAP suggests time off from any one sport each year.
Off-season (rest of it)Fix your biggest weakness3–4Weak foot, strength routine, the mistake your match reviews kept showing.
Pre-season (last 4–6 weeks)Be fit for day one3–4Build running and sprints a little each week, keep touches and game IQ going.

The 12-week plan above fits neatly into an off-season plus pre-season, or into the first half of a season if you keep the in-season limits.

faq_add.q: How long should a solo soccer training session be?
faq_add.a: Most solo sessions work well at 20 to 45 minutes. One longer session of about 45 minutes mid-week plus two short ones of 10 to 20 minutes is enough for most players who also train with a team.

faq_add.q: What equipment do I need to train soccer alone?
faq_add.a: A ball, a wall or rebounder, a few cones or markers, a phone for timing and filming, and about 20 metres of flat space. You don't need a gym or special gear to follow a solid plan.

faq_add.q: How should I train in the soccer off-season?
faq_add.a: Take some time off first and play other sports. Then spend the rest of the off-season on your biggest weakness, a strength routine and gradual fitness, building up over the last 4 to 6 weeks before pre-season.

faq_add.q: Do soccer players need strength training?
faq_add.a: Yes, a short bodyweight routine two or three times a week helps. A 2008 trial of 1,892 young female players found a structured warm-up for strength and control lowered overall and severe injuries over a season.
